verdicts.trueWording: "and to rewrite Silas's speech, all broken monosyllables"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched: ebin.pub scan of Dancing at the Edge of the World, essay "Reciprocity of Prose and Poetry" (1983). Quote "all broken monosyllables" appears word for word in the paragraph beginning "That the subject of that passage has an identity and interest apart from the words is true...". Every limb holds: the passage is George Eliot's (endnote 4 cites Silas Marner, Harcourt 1962, p.140), the speaker is Silas, and Le Guin's argument there is precisely inseparability of word and idea -- she offers the rewrite as something that ought to be easy if word and idea were separable, then denies it is easy or possible and calls tampering with the passage offensive. Locator quibble only, not a claim limb: the sentence sits below the running head "io8 URSULA K. LEGUIN" and above the running head "RECIPROCITY OF PROSE AND POETRY 109", so it is p.108, one page earlier than the chunk's "p.109".

verdicts.trueWording: "They talk too much. They explain things too much."
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from themillions.com (HTTP 200); byline and date on the page are Paul Morton, January 31, 2013, matching the source field. Quote appears word for word, immediately after "I was re-reading The Lathe of Heaven -- which I'm still fond of, which I still think is funny -- but, boy would I cut it if I could." The referent of "They" is the novel's characters, and Le Guin's own earlier novel is named on the page, so both limbs hold. Minor locator quibble only: it falls in the answer about Taoist "doing not-doing", roughly two-thirds through, not "near the end".

verdicts.trueWording: "in the most conventional, banal prose, if the writer has the gift"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from ursulakleguin.com blog 51, "The Narrative Gift as a Moral Conundrum" (HTTP 200). The full sentence in the paragraph beginning "Inept writing lames or cripples good narrative only if it's truly inept" reads word for word as the chunk quotes it, continuing ", if the writer has the gift." The claim's "narrative gift" limb is supported: the page says "the gift" and the essay's title and opening line ("The narrative gift, is that what to call it?") fix the referent. Source-metadata correction, not a claim limb: the post is dated May 2012 on the page (byline "May 1, 2012", opening "May 2012 (Reading, Seeing ii)"), not 2011.

verdicts.trueWording: "Art isn't explanation. Art is what an artist does"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from ursulakleguin.com blog 36, "Readers' Questions", dated October 2011 on the page, matching the source field. The quoted words appear verbatim (curly apostrophe in the original) and the very next clause supplies the claim's second limb: "Art is what an artist does, not what an artist explains." It sits in the paragraph contrasting a reviewer's job with a fiction writer's, just before the potter analogy.

verdicts.trueWording: "I wasn't choosing the way as an author, I was taking dictation"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from lithub.com (HTTP 200); byline Euan Monaghan, April 1, 2016, matching the source field (the page also states the interview first appeared in Structo Magazine issue 14). The quote is word for word in Le Guin's answer to the opening question "Lavinia was your most recent novel... how it came about", so the Lavinia limb holds. The page continues ", as it were -- finding the story as it happened", a hedge the claim does not carry but does not contradict.

Raw page fetched from publicbooks.org (HTTP 200). The sentence appears twice, as a pull quote and in the body: "In pure, ignorant defiance of the decree of the Iowa Writing School that controls almost all modern fiction, Galt tells without showing." Both limbs hold -- the Iowa Writing School decree is Le Guin's own phrasing, and the praise limb is explicit in the preceding sentence, "Having read that sentence, I was in love with the book", as well as in the article's standfirst about a novel that "blissfully tells without showing".

verdicts.trueWording: "a hard and sore time of it with such an outstrapolous people"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from publicbooks.org. Le Guin writes: "All he says about it is, 'I thought I would have a hard and sore time of it with such an outstrapolous people.'" The quoted words are verbatim and the "entire account" limb is supported by her own framing "All he says about it is". Nuance worth recording, not a defect in the claim: she then adds a second Galt quotation ("And: 'After the ceremony, we then got out at the window...'"), so "entire account of the riot" is her characterisation of Balwhidder's comment on the riot itself, not a count of every Galt sentence she reproduces. The riot is at his installation as minister of Dalmailing, as the claim says.

verdicts.trueWording: "without even a period, only a semicolon"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from publicbooks.org. The paragraph after the block quotation reads "And immediately, without even a period, only a semicolon, 'we went to the manse, and there we had an excellent dinner ...'", following Galt's "We then got out at the window, and it was a heavy day to me." Quote is verbatim and both limbs hold: the annalist is Mr. Balwhidder, whose year-by-year annals Le Guin is describing, and the movement is from the riot's aftermath straight to the dinner.

verdicts.trueWording: "dry, subtle, morally loaded, and really funny"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from publicbooks.org. Verbatim in the Austen-comparison paragraph: "But his humor, though softer, is like hers -- dry, subtle, morally loaded, and really funny." The page locator in the chunk is exact; "hers" is Jane Austen's, and the four adjectives are applied to Galt's humour as the claim states.

verdicts.trueWording: "it becomes a jargon, meaningful only to an ingroup"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from theguardian.com (HTTP 200), article "The stars of modern SF pick the best science fiction". Le Guin's contribution, headed "Virginia Woolf (1882-1941)", carries the whole claim verbatim in its first paragraph: "Genre is a rich dialect, in which you can say certain things in a particularly satisfying way, but if it gives up connection with the general literary language it becomes a jargon, meaningful only to an ingroup." All limbs supported. The page's timestamp reads Fri 13 May 2011 19.06 EDT, i.e. 14 May 2011 UK time as the source field gives.

verdicts.trueWording: "a matter of language and names; it has rules"
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched from locusmag.com (HTTP 200), "Frankenstein's Earthsea", Locus January 2005 (mailing date 30 December 2004 on the page). Verbatim in the second of the three assumptions she attacks: "In the 'Earthsea' books the way magic works is quite specific, a matter of language and names; it has rules, which give it a necessary limitation; and the nature of this magic is one of the fundamental metaphors on which the story is built." Both limbs supported, and the location is indeed the discussion of the film's changes.

Raw page fetched from locusmag.com, same sentence as index 922. The relative clause attaches to "it has rules", so the claim's limb -- that it is the rules that give the magic a necessary limitation -- is exactly what the page says. Verbatim.
